---
title: "Colloids, surfaces, and sorption exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Double the solid

Repeat the worked example with 0.0200 kg solid, keeping all other inputs fixed. Find aqueous concentration and both inventories.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use the full denominator, not a proportional guess.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Cw = 1/(1 + 100 × 0.0200) = **0.3333 mg/L**. Water holds **0.3333 mg**, solid **0.6667 mg**. The sorbed concentration is 33.33 mg/kg and the total remains 1.00 mg.
:::

## 2. A loading limit

A solid has qmax = 20.0 mg/kg and dry mass 0.0100 kg. Can it bind 1.00 mg on those sites?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Multiply capacity by dry solid mass.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The maximum site inventory is **0.200 mg**, so 1.00 mg cannot all bind there. More solid, other retention mechanisms, or a larger aqueous pool would be required.
:::

## 3. A desorption change

A new pH changes Kd in the original bottle from 100 to 10.0 L/kg. At equilibrium with the same total mass and volume, what is Cw?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Changing Kd redistributes the fixed inventory.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Cw = 1/(1 + 10 × 0.0100) = **0.9091 mg/L**. Aqueous mass is 0.9091 mg and sorbed mass 0.09091 mg. Desorption raised the water concentration without adding total solute.
:::

## 4. Removal or transport?

A filtered sample loses metal while the unfiltered downstream sample does not. How could particles explain this observation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Compare operational fractions and whether particles settle or remain mobile.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Metal may bind to particles excluded by filtration while remaining in the moving water-plus-particle system. Measure particle loads, size fractions, flow, and phase inventories. A filtered concentration decrease alone does not establish destruction or permanent retention.
:::

## Explore: the two-phase bottle {#explore}

Predict what happens to the water concentration if you double the solid while
keeping the solute and water fixed. Then predict what a tenfold drop in K~d~,
for example after a pH change, does to the mass on the solid.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="sorption" role="group" aria-label="Water–solid distribution in a closed bottle">
<p>Reference case: 1.00 mg solute, 1.00 L water, 0.0100 kg solid and K<sub>d</sub> = 100 L/kg give 0.500 mg/L in water and 0.500 mg on the solid.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/sorption.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Worked example**, then **Double the solid**. Check both water
concentrations by hand with C~w~ = M~T~/(V~w~ + K~d~m~s~). Why is the second
one a third, not a quarter?

**E2.** Choose **pH change: Kd falls to 10**. How much solute moved from the
solid back into the water? Was any solute added?

**E3.** Reset, then find the solid mass at which exactly half the solute is
sorbed for K~d~ = 20 L/kg. Explain your answer using the idea of an "extra
volume" K~d~m~s~.

### Model conditions and hand check

For the worked example, K~d~m~s~ = 100 × 0.0100 = 1.00 L, so
C~w~ = 1.00/(1.00 + 1.00) = **0.500 mg/L**. The water holds 0.500 mg, the
solid 0.500 mg, and q = 50.0 mg/kg. With 0.0200 kg solid, C~w~ = 1/3.00 =
**0.333 mg/L**. With K~d~ = 10 L/kg, C~w~ = 1/1.10 = **0.909 mg/L**.

The bottle is closed and at equilibrium. Sorption is linear (q = K~d~C~w~),
so there is no capacity limit; a real solid holds at most q~max~ × m~s~.
K~d~ is set by hand: the demo does not calculate how pH changes it.
There is no degradation, loss to the walls, or competition from other solutes.
The comparison curve uses a K~d~ ten times smaller than the current one.
